The 1089 Trick

Place ValueArithmeticAlgebra
Game: Turn a number backwards, take away the smaller from the bigger, then add the answer to its own backwards version. There is nothing to win — watch what always happens.
How to play: Click the left or right half of a blue digit to lower or raise it. Change the base, the number of digits or the link between digits, then press New number for another try.

Answer

Tap the left half of a blue digit to make it smaller, or the right half to make it bigger. Arrow keys work too; a wide number slides sideways.

Look for the math

Start with 732, turn it around to get 237, take away 237 from 732 to get 495, then add 495 to its own reversal 594. The answer is 1089. Try any other three digits: the same thing happens. Why?

The middle digit is always nine

Write the starting number as 100a + 10b + c. Turned around it is 100c + 10b + a, so taking the smaller from the larger removes the middle digit entirely: the difference is 99(a − c). Borrowing one hundred rewrites that as 100(a − c − 1) + 90 + (10 + c − a). In other words the difference has the shape x9y, where the two outside digits add up to nine. A palindrome (a = c) gives zero instead.

Adding a number to its reversal

The reversal of x9y is y9x. Adding them digit by digit gives 100(x + y) + 90 + 90 + (x + y). Since x + y = 9, that is 900 + 180 + 9 = 1089. Nothing in the sum depends on which number you started with — only on having three places and a nonzero difference. With two digits the same argument gives 99; with one digit it gives zero. The applet pads the difference with a leading zero before reversing it, so 100 − 1 = 099 reverses to 990, not 99.

It works in any base

In positional notation with base b, exactly the same steps give b³ + b² − b − 1, written as 10uv, where u = b − 2 and v = b − 1 are the two largest digits. Base ten gives 1089; base thirty-six gives 10YZ. Change the base on the page to see it happen. The logic test checks every three-digit number in every base from 2 to 36.

What was checked

The page's claims all held: 1089 for three digits, 99 for two, zero for a palindrome, and 10uv in every base. The test compares the core with a second transcription of the applet's own method over about 460,000 positions and of its digit-clicking code in every case for bases 2 to 12. Two applet quirks are kept: a wrapped digit chooses its carry direction from its old value (so in base two, clicking up on a zero borrows), and a new random number that is too big for a 64-bit integer leaves the old number in place. One quirk is not kept: reversing all zeroes makes the Java applet delete past the end of its buffer, while the page says the sum is zero, so this page shows zero.

Set the base to 2 and try 101, then switch Autonomous digits on and click a wrapped digit. What changes?
